title: Mining of Mineral Resources
summary: South Africa's mineral resources, methods of mining, extracting and refining minerals, and the economic, social and environmental effects of mining.

notes.text: A naturally occurring, solid, non-living substance with a definite chemical composition, found in the Earth's crust.
Rock that contains enough of a valuable mineral to make it worth mining.
South Africa is one of the world's richest countries in mineral resources. Minerals are **non-renewable**: once they are mined, they cannot be replaced.

rows: Ore near the surface is dug out after removing the soil and rock above it, leaving a large pit
Coal, iron ore, diamonds (the Big Hole in Kimberley)
Vertical shafts and horizontal tunnels reach deep ore bodies; some gold mines are over 3 km deep
Minerals are sieved from river gravels and beach sands
Long strips of overburden are removed and replaced after mining

notes.title: Choosing a mining method
notes.problem: Coal lies in a thick layer 40 m underground. Gold ore lies in a narrow band 3 km down. Which method suits each?
steps: If the deposit is near the surface, removing what lies on top is cheapest: open-cast mining.
At 3 km it is impossible to remove the rock above, so shafts and tunnels are needed.
notes.answer: Open-cast for the coal; deep underground mining for the gold.

items: **Extraction**: ore is blasted and removed from the ground.
**Crushing and milling**: the ore is broken into small pieces or powder.
**Separation**: the mineral is separated from waste rock, for example with chemicals (cyanide is used to dissolve gold), flotation or magnets.
**Refining**: the metal is purified, often by heating to very high temperatures (smelting).
The waste rock is dumped as **mine dumps** and **tailings** (fine waste in slime dams).

notes.title: How much gold from the ore?
notes.problem: A mine's ore contains 5 g of gold per tonne. How much gold comes from 1 000 tonnes of ore?
steps: Nearly all of the 1 000 tonnes is waste rock, which is why mine dumps are so large.

rows: Creates jobs for hundreds of thousands of people
Dangerous work: rock falls, underground fires, lung diseases such as silicosis and TB
Destroys habitats and scars the landscape
Acid mine drainage pollutes rivers and groundwater
Towns and infrastructure are built around mines
Dust and toxic waste from dumps; air pollution from smelters
Migrant labour separates families; towns may die when mines close

notes.label: Key idea
notes.text: **Rehabilitation** means restoring land after mining: filling pits, replacing topsoil and replanting indigenous vegetation. South African law requires mining companies to plan and pay for rehabilitation.

questions.memo:
✓ Water flowing through old mines and dumps becomes acidic and carries dissolved metals (1)
✓ It pollutes rivers and groundwater, harming plants, animals and people who use the water (1)

questions.prompt: Discuss TWO positive and TWO negative effects of mining on South Africa.
questions.memo:
Positive (1 each): jobs; exports/foreign income; raw materials; infrastructure; tax revenue
Negative (1 each): dangerous work and lung disease; habitat destruction; water pollution; dust and dumps; migrant labour

questions.prompt: Describe how mined land can be rehabilitated.
questions.memo: Any two (1 each): fill in pits and level the land; replace topsoil; replant indigenous plants; clean up waste dumps and treat polluted water

questions.prompt: Name the steps, in order, by which a metal is obtained from its ore.
questions.memo:
✓ Extraction/mining (1)
✓ Crushing and separating the mineral from waste rock (1)
✓ Refining/smelting to purify the metal (1)
